The optimal timeliness/cost tradeoff is achieved by averaging embeddings over the most recent SIX MONTHS; gross Sharpe stays near 3.0 for lookbacks up to 6 months and falls to 2.4 at 24 months.
key_findings.numbers: ~30%/yr on 10% vol, no delay; predictability halves after 1 month; insignificant only after ~18 months; turnover 75% one-sided vs JKP max 67%; assumed cost 10bp/dollar traded; optimal lookback = 6 months; Sharpe ~3.0 up to 6-month lookback, 2.4 at 24 months; Sharpe 3.1 overall 1996-2022 vs max JKP anomaly 1.4

key_findings.claim: BREADTH, not large-cap efficiency, is what caps this channel — and it caps it near Sharpe 1.4-1.5 for a universe of our size. The pure-news portfolio earns Sharpe 2.7 among small stocks but only 1.4 among large stocks (above the NYSE 50th percentile, averaging 832 stocks/month). A bootstrap that resamples N firms/month shows the large-cap shortfall is a cross-sectional-breadth effect: at matched N the bootstrap Sharpe is 1.5, essentially equal to the 1.4 realized on large caps. pyfinagent's 500-1000 name universe sits exactly at this point, so ~1.4-1.5 gross Sharpe is the realistic ceiling from a news/theme channel before costs and before publication decay. Critically, the paper also reports the news anomaly does NOT decay late in sample, explicitly contrasting itself with McLean and Pontiff (2016).
key_findings.numbers: Sharpe 2.7 small / 1.4 large; large subsample averages 832 stocks; bootstrap at matched N gives 1.5; small-N bootstrap Sharpe 0.5; best JKP large-stock factor well below; 4,198 stocks/month, 52.5% have news in a given month, average 4.6 articles/month

key_findings.claim: ATTENTION IS AN EXIT SIGNAL, NOT AN ENTRY SIGNAL — and it is null in our universe. Da, Engelberg and Gao find a Google SVI spike predicts +11 bps per WEEK for the first two weeks, but ONLY among SMALL Russell 3000 stocks (annualizing to ~5.7%); the outperformance 'stops after two weeks' and is 'completely reversed within the first year after portfolio formation'. There is no significant effect in the large-cap third — a direct null for an S&P500/Russell1000 universe. In IPOs, SVI jumps 80% (median) during the IPO week and reverts to its pre-IPO level within two weeks; high-SVI IPOs earn 17.25% first-day versus 10.48% for low-SVI (difference 6.78%, significant at 1%), and then reverse long-run. Retail attention spikes are a two-week overreaction followed by reversal, so peak attention marks the top, not the entry.
key_findings.numbers: +11 bps/week for 2 weeks, small stocks only, ~5.7% annualized; fully reversed within 1 year; null in large-cap third; IPO SVI +80% median, reverts in 2 weeks; first-day 17.25% vs 10.48%, diff 6.78% (sig at 1%); Russell 3000, Jan 2004-Jun 2008

key_findings.claim: POST-NEWS DRIFT IS ASYMMETRIC AND SITS ON THE SHORT SIDE — the long side, which is all a paper-trading book can use, is weak. Chan (2003) finds a news long-short cumulative 3-factor alpha of 6.2% at 12 months (CAPM 5.8%, t=4.7; raw ~6%). But decomposed with size/book-to-market adjustment at 12 months, news WINNERS earn only +1.7% (significant at just the 10% level) while news LOSERS earn -3.3% (5% level); CAPM news-loser CAR is -7.8% at 12 months (t=2.5). The paper states 'all of the news winner drift is due to post earnings drift' and concludes 'investors primarily underreact to bad news'. Separately, extreme price moves WITHOUT news REVERSE in month 1: no-news losers recover +0.7% after a -13.7% drop, no-news winners give back -0.6% after a +16.3% run-up, then go flat. Long-run, gains reverse 'around the two-year mark or beyond' and are 'almost eliminated'. Effects apply mainly to smaller stocks (1980-1999, ~1500 stocks).
key_findings.numbers: news L/S 3-factor CAR 6.2% at 12m; CAPM 5.8% (t=4.7); news winners +1.7% (10% sig) vs news losers -3.3% (5% sig) size/BM-adjusted at 12m; news losers CAPM -7.8% (t=2.5); no-news losers +0.7% after -13.7%; no-news winners -0.6% after +16.3%; reversal by year 2

key_findings.claim: STALE NEWS PRODUCES OVERREACTION THAT REVERSES — so counting ARTICLE VOLUME buys the reversal. Tetlock defines staleness as a story's textual similarity to the previous ten stories about the same firm. The market's initial reaction to news in the BOTTOM staleness decile exceeds its reaction to the TOP staleness decile by 413 bps equal-weighted (75 bps value-weighted). Staleness-sorted portfolios then show return reversals differing by 26 bps in the week after news (15 bps VW), i.e. the market revises its initial view by 26/413 = 6.3% EW (19.8% in percentage terms VW). The reversal is significantly larger in stocks with above-average individual-investor trading. Implication: a theme signal built on raw article counts will systematically load on repetition of already-priced stories; novelty must be measured, not volume.
key_findings.numbers: initial reaction gap fresh-vs-stale 413 bps EW / 75 bps VW; subsequent one-week reversal gap 26 bps EW / 15 bps VW; revision 6.3% EW, 19.8% VW; reversal larger where individual-investor trading above average; published RFS 2011, 24(5), 1481-1512

key_findings.claim: POST-PUBLICATION DECAY, and the specific warning that it is WORST in exactly our universe. The published McLean and Pontiff (2016, JF 71:5-32) study of 97 predictor variables finds portfolio returns 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication, implying ~32% attributable to publication-informed trading. The earlier working draft I read in full (82 characteristics) reports a smaller ~35% post-publication decay with a statistical bias of ~10% that is NOT significant (out-of-sample return 78% of in-sample, t=-1.40; post-publication 51% of in-sample, t=-4.91; panel estimates 42%, 37%, 34%), giving a lower bound on the pure publication effect of about 25%. The load-bearing conditional result: 'the post-publication decline is greatest for anomalies that are concentrated in large market capitalization stocks, high dollar volume stocks, low idiosyncratic risk stocks, and stocks that pay dividends' — i.e. an S&P500/Russell1000 implementation should expect the HIGH end of the decay range, not the average. Variance, turnover, dollar volume and short interest all rise post-publication.
key_findings.numbers: Published: 97 variables, 26% lower out-of-sample, 58% lower post-publication (=> ~32% publication effect). Working draft: 82 characteristics, ~35% decay, 10% bias (n.s.), OOS 78% of in-sample (t=-1.40), post-pub 51% (t=-4.91), panel 42%/37%/34%, lower bound ~25%. Decay greatest in large-cap, high-dollar-volume, low-idio-risk, dividend-paying stocks

key_findings.claim: GRADUAL INFORMATION DIFFUSION across markets is real but SLOW and NARROW — the cross-asset lead is measured in ONE TO TWO MONTHS, which sets the outer bound on how early a second-order signal can be harvested. Hong, Torous and Valkanov find that over 1946-2002, fourteen of thirty-four US industries (including commercial real estate, petroleum, metal, retail, financial, services) predict market movements by one month, and a subset (petroleum, metal, financial) forecast two months ahead. This survives controls for risk/liquidity proxies and lagged market returns. Simulations show only 0.04% of random draws produce fourteen or more forecasting industries, and on average only five would do so by chance at the 10% level. An industry's ability to lead the market correlates with its ability to forecast industrial production growth, supporting the gradual-diffusion (Hong-Stein) mechanism rather than pure statistical artifact. Results replicate in the eight largest non-US markets (1973-2002).
key_findings.numbers: 14 of 34 US industries predict market 1 month ahead; petroleum/metal/financial predict 2 months ahead; only 0.04% of simulations produce >=14 by chance; ~5 expected by chance at the 10% level; 1946-2002 US, 1973-2002 for 8 non-US markets

negative_or_null_results: NULL — Google/SVI attention has NO significant effect in large-cap stocks. Da/Engelberg/Gao's +11bps/week result holds 'only among small Russell stocks'; the large third shows nothing. Any SVI or search-attention entry trigger is dead on arrival for an S&P500/Russell1000 universe.

NULL — selecting theme beneficiaries by MEDIA COVERAGE produces zero alpha. Lee/Ozik/Sadka Table 7: narrative-mimicking portfolios formed from the top-25 highest-media-coverage stocks regardless of beta 'do not exhibit abnormal returns'. Only return-beta selection works. This directly invalidates 'ask an LLM which companies are named as benefiting'.

NEGATIVE — buying the top-5 holdings of newly launched specialized ETFs LOSES money at a magnitude similar to the ETFs themselves (Ben-David et al., Appendix Table F.6). This is the closest published analogue to a naive theme->beneficiary basket and it is negative.

NEGATIVE — theme/sector ETF launch is followed by reversal of the entire pre-launch run-up, whereas smart-beta launches merely flatten to zero alpha. The reversal is specific to the sector/thematic (attention-driven) category, confirming it is overvaluation rather than generic overfitting.

NEGATIVE — ranking candidates by recent run-up plus positive media sentiment is an ANTI-signal at 6-60 month horizons: the highest pre-launch return/sentiment specialized ETFs deliver -0.53%/mo FFC4 vs -0.20%/mo for the lowest.

NULL — a 1-YEAR customer return is not a usable sorting variable on a value-weighted basis: 0.694%/mo, t=1.85, insignificant (it survives equal-weighted at 1.13%, t=4.16). The second-order signal is a RECENT shock to the linked firm, not a slow 12-month trend. Since our universe is large/mid-cap, the value-weighted (insignificant) read is the relevant one.

NULL/NEGATIVE — 1-week and 3-month narrative intensity differences do NOT generate the spread; only the 6-month intensity difference does ('the narrative spread portfolio has positive returns when sorted by 6-month intensity differences'). Short-window theme-attention changes are not tradable at this horizon.

NEGATIVE — the long side of post-news drift is weak. Chan's size/BM-adjusted 12-month news-winner CAR is only +1.7% (10% significance) and the author states all of it is post-earnings-announcement drift; the economically large effect (-3.3% to -7.8%) is on the SHORT side. A long-biased paper book captures the weak half of this anomaly.

NEGATIVE — extreme price moves WITHOUT news reverse in the following month (no-news losers +0.7% after -13.7%; no-news winners -0.6% after +16.3%) and then produce essentially zero thereafter. Price-move-only theme detection with no news confirmation is a reversal trade, not a drift trade.

NEGATIVE — the fast news strategy is cost-hostile: 75% one-sided turnover exceeds EVERY factor in the Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen universe (highest is short-term reversal at 67%). This independently confirms the operator's decision to rule out fast headline-drift trading.

NEGATIVE — post-publication decay is GREATEST for anomalies concentrated in large-cap, high-dollar-volume, low-idiosyncratic-risk, dividend-paying stocks. pyfinagent's universe is the worst case for anomaly decay, not the average case.

CONTRADICTION WORTH FLAGGING — Didisheim/Kelly et al. (2026) report the pure-news anomaly shows no decay late in sample, explicitly contrasting McLean and Pontiff (2016). Two credible sources disagree on whether this specific channel decays. The 2026 result is new and unpublished; do not rely on it.

VERSION DISCREPANCY — the McLean/Pontiff working draft I read in full reports ~35% post-publication decay from 82 characteristics with a statistically INSIGNIFICANT 10% out-of-sample bias, while the published 2016 JF version reports 97 variables, 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication. Citing '58%' as if it were the draft's finding would be wrong; both are reported above.

NOTE — Ben-David et al. specialized-ETF underperformance is statistically indistinguishable from zero AFTER month 60 (-0.12%/mo, t=-1.56). Crowding damage is bounded in time; it is not a permanent impairment of the theme.
recommendation_for_pyfinagent: ENTRY (acceleration, never birth or confirmation): trigger on a POSITIVE and RISING 6-MONTH theme attention-intensity difference (trailing 6-month mean intensity minus the prior 6-month mean) — not article counts, not 1-week spikes, not price run-up. Build this at CYCLE level from Alpha Vantage NEWS_SENTIMENT (the only present key), which satisfies the $0 and cost-control constraints because theme extraction is one pass over ~50-100 themes per cycle rather than per-ticker. BENEFICIARY SELECTION must be by 6-month rolling RETURN BETA of each stock to the theme-intensity series, NOT by an LLM naming who benefits and NOT by article mentions — the media-coverage selection method is a published null (Lee/Ozik/Sadka Table 7) and is the same method that produces the -30%/5yr ETF result. Use the LLM only to define and label the theme vocabulary (cycle-level), and let statistics pick the names. EXCLUDE the first-order named firm entirely (URC 0.939 — no residual drift to harvest). EXIT: hard exit at 6 months (the C&F second-order gap closes over t+1..t+6; the narrative signal is calibrated at a 6-month holding horizon; the news anomaly's optimal lookback is 6 months), absolute cap 12 months (C&F: 'persist for about a year and then fade away'; Chan drift reverses by year 2). CROWDING KILL-SWITCH, forced regardless of holding age, on ANY of: (a) a thematic/sector ETF launching on the theme; (b) the theme's attention-intensity difference turning negative — descending-attention narratives are the SHORT leg of the 7%/yr spread, so holding one is actively adverse; (c) basket media sentiment rolling over from its peak. This maps cleanly onto the existing sign_safe_mult overlay pattern as a multiplicative veto rather than a new engine. INFRASTRUCTURE PREREQUISITE — this is the blocking item: 0 of the 37 _NUMERIC_FEATURES are news-derived and bq_writer targets news_articles/news_sentiment tables that DO NOT EXIST (fail-open, silent no-op). Until the corpus is persisted and the theme-intensity + theme-beta features are exposed to the backtest engine, this signal cannot be gated at all and must not be allowed to move live trades. Create the tables and wire the features BEFORE any promotion attempt. EXPECTED ECONOMICS, stated conservatively: start from ~7%/yr gross theme alpha (t=2.53), of which only ~1.5%/yr is genuinely cross-sector (the rest is intra-sector, already partly covered by peer_leadlag_screen); apply the McLean-Pontiff large-cap-worst-case decay (58% published / 35-42% draft) to get roughly 2-4%/yr gross of costs; note the achievable Sharpe ceiling for a ~800-name universe is about 1.4-1.5 by the bootstrap. Size the DSR>=0.95 / PBO<=0.5 expectation against 2-4%/yr, not 7%.
rejected_options: Fast headline-drift / news-shock trading — rejected on measured turnover: 75% one-sided exceeds every JKP factor (max 67% for short-term reversal), and the SVI attention effect lasts only 2 weeks, is small-cap-only, and fully reverses within a year. Independently confirms the operator's existing out-of-scope decision.

LLM-names-the-beneficiary theme mapping — rejected on a direct published null: media-coverage-selected narrative portfolios show no abnormal returns, while beta-selected ones earn 6.96%/yr. The LLM should define themes, not pick stocks.

Buying or tracking thematic ETFs, or their top holdings, after launch — rejected: -0.50%/mo FFC4 (t=-4.02) for 60 months, ~-30% cumulative, and the stock-level top-5-holdings variant underperforms similarly.

Trading the first-order, directly-named firm — rejected: underreaction coefficient 0.939 (t=1.53, indistinguishable from 1) and insignificant post-event CAR (+0.442%, t=1.59). The move is already priced in the event month.
Google Trends / SVI as an entry trigger — rejected: null in large caps, which is our entire universe.

Article-volume or coverage-count as the theme intensity metric — rejected: Tetlock shows repetition (staleness) drives overreaction that reverses (413bps initial gap, 26bps one-week reversal gap); volume measures repetition, not information.
Ranking beneficiaries by recent price run-up plus positive media sentiment — rejected: this is the exact profile of the worst-performing specialized ETFs (-0.53%/mo).
A 1-year (slow-trend) linked-firm return as the sorting signal — rejected: insignificant value-weighted (0.694%/mo, t=1.85).

Long-only reliance on good-news drift — rejected: size/BM-adjusted news-winner drift is only +1.7% at 12 months (10% significance) and is entirely post-earnings drift; the real effect is on the short side we cannot take.

Reusing peer_leadlag_screen.py for the cross-sector hop — rejected structurally: it groups by GICS sector, but 78% of the exploitable economic links are cross-industry. It cannot express the mechanism.

Building the signal before persisting the news corpus and adding news features to _NUMERIC_FEATURES — rejected on governance: with zero news features in the backtest engine the signal is un-gate-able against DSR/PBO, which violates the immutable promotion-gate requirement.
open_questions: BIGGEST FEASIBILITY RISK — sample length. Alpha Vantage NEWS_SENTIMENT is confirmed back only to about 2022-02-24, giving ~4.5 years. A 6-month-holding, 6-month-signal strategy has roughly 9 non-overlapping periods in that window. Can that clear DSR>=0.95 and PBO<=0.5 at all? The published results use 2013-2023 (Lee/Ozik/Sadka) and 1996-2022 (Didisheim et al.). If the answer is no, the honest conclusion is that this signal cannot be promoted under our own gates regardless of its economic merit, and the step should be scoped as research-only.

Does the 6-month narrative-intensity result survive on a $0 corpus? The published result uses 150k+ sources at 5-7 million articles/week; Alpha Vantage is orders of magnitude thinner. The bootstrap in Didisheim et al. shows Sharpe scales strongly with cross-sectional breadth (0.5 at small N rising to ~1.5 at N=832) — an analogous corpus-breadth sensitivity is plausible and untested.

Can a point-in-time thematic-ETF launch registry be obtained at $0 without look-ahead bias? The crowding kill-switch depends on it. ETF_PROFILE exists on Alpha Vantage but inception-date coverage and as-of correctness are unverified.

Is the genuinely cross-sector component (1.46%/yr, t=2.59) large enough to clear costs standalone, given that the intra-sector component (4.69%/yr) is partly already captured by the existing peer_leadlag_screen overlay? The true INCREMENT over the current book may be much smaller than 7%/yr.

Does the 2026 'no late-sample decay' finding for pure news survive peer review and replication? It directly contradicts McLean-Pontiff for this channel and would materially change the expected-alpha haircut if true. It is currently an unpublished NBER working paper (April 2026, revised May 2026).

Do the four operator reference cases (COVID, AI/datacenter, Ukraine, Iran/oil) actually register as rising 6-month intensity differences BEFORE the second-order names moved, or only contemporaneously? This is directly testable on the Alpha Vantage archive for the AI/datacenter and Iran/oil cases (both post-2022) but NOT for COVID or Ukraine's onset, which predate the archive — meaning two of the four reference cases cannot be backtested at all on free data.

Chan (2003), Cohen-Frazzini (2008) and Da et al. (2011) all report their effects concentrate in smaller and less liquid stocks. How much of the second-order edge survives at all in a strictly large/mid-cap universe? C&F is reassuring (same total alpha, faster convergence) but Chan and Da are not.

lens: LENS 4 — Cost and turnover: does the edge survive?
bottom_line: For a $0-metered, ~$100k, long-only book in S&P-500-grade names, cost scales exactly linearly with turnover: annual cost (bps) = T × c, where T = 2 × rebalances/yr × fraction-of-book-replaced and c = one-way cost in bps. At a defensible c = 3 bps, a weeks-to-months thematic design costs 6–39 bps/yr and a daily headline design costs 1,382 bps/yr — a 35x difference against an empirically realistic large-cap alpha budget of only 48–240 bps/yr. The crossover sits at T ≈ 16–80x/yr (roughly a 3-week to 6-week minimum holding period); slow thematic designs clear it by 2–10x, daily headline designs miss it by ~20x. Cost is therefore NOT the binding constraint on the slow thematic channel — alpha is — and the next research cycle should not be spent on cost engineering.

key_findings.claim: Novy-Marx & Velikov's headline turnover threshold: anomalies with under 50% one-sided MONTHLY turnover mostly survive costs; almost none above it do. Their Table 3 (value-weighted decile long-shorts, 1963-2012) splits cleanly by bucket: LOW turnover (annual rebalance, one-sided TO 1.23%-7.24%/mo) costs 3-11 bps/mo and every strategy keeps its gross spread; MID (monthly, TO 14.36%-35.07%/mo) costs 20-65 bps/mo and only 5 of 9 stay significant net; HIGH (TO 90.1%-94.0%/mo) costs 106-178 bps/mo and 4 of 6 go NEGATIVE net.
key_findings.numbers: Low: Gross Profitability net 0.37%/mo t=2.74 (TO 1.96, cost 3bp); ValProf net 0.77 t=4.82; Investment net 0.46 t=3.60; Value net 0.42 t=2.39. Mid: ValMomProf net 0.99 t=5.18 (TO 26.81, cost 43bp); Momentum net 0.68 t=2.45 (TO 34.52, cost 65bp); PEAD-CAR3 net 0.34 t=2.41; but IdioVol net 0.11 t=0.37, Failure Prob net 0.24 t=0.73, PEAD-SUE net 0.26 t=1.60, ROE net 0.33 t=1.38 all DIE. High: Industry Momentum net -0.29 t=-1.20; Industry Rel Reversals net -0.80 t=-4.73; Short-run Reversals net -1.28 t=-6.02; Seasonality net -0.62 t=-3.88. Rule of thumb stated verbatim: costs 'reduce realized spreads by more than 1% of the monthly one-sided turnover'. Round-trip costs 'average in excess of 50 bps'; EW strategies 'two to three times as high'.

key_findings.claim: Ke/Kelly/Xiu's newswire strategy is profitable net of costs ONLY equal-weighted. Their Table 5 (the sole net-of-cost table) is explicitly 'equally-weighted long-short EWCT portfolios'. Their VALUE-WEIGHTED portfolio — the large-cap-relevant one for us — is never given a net-of-cost line, and applying their OWN 10 bps cost convention (verified to reproduce Table 5 exactly on all rows) makes it deeply loss-making. This is the single most decision-relevant number in the lens.
key_findings.numbers: Table 2 (OOS Feb 2004-Jul 2017, Dow Jones Newswires x CRSP): EW L-S Sharpe 4.29, daily turnover 94.6%, gross 33 bps/day. VW L-S Sharpe 1.33, daily turnover 91.4%, gross 10 bps/day; VW short leg gross 1 bp/day, Sharpe 0.04. Table 5 cost convention = 2 x turnover x 10bps (verified exactly: gamma=0.5 gross 20.43 - net 11.23 = 9.20 = 2x0.46x10; gamma=0.9 diff 17.00 = 2x0.85x10; gamma=0.1 diff 1.60). Applying it to the VW row: cost = 2x0.914x10 = 18.28 bps/day vs 10 bps/day gross => DERIVED net -8.28 bps/day (~-21%/yr). Table 5 EW net Sharpe peaks at 2.30 at gamma=0.5 (turnover 0.46/day, gross SR 4.26) — costs cut Sharpe 46%; at gamma=0.9 net SR 1.92 vs gross 4.37, a 56% haircut. Even the most-constrained row (gamma=0.1) is 0.08 daily turnover = ~20x NAV/yr. The 10bps assumption is cited to Frazzini et al. (2018).

key_findings.claim: The honest expected-return budget for ANY new signal in a value-weighted large-cap universe is ~48 bps/YEAR, not the 8%/yr the anomaly literature advertises. Chen & Velikov net out spreads, post-publication decay and the post-2005 trading regime across 120 anomalies and find the average cost-optimized value-weighted anomaly expects 4 bps/month with SE 3 bps — statistically indistinguishable from zero. This is the denominator every turnover budget must be measured against.
key_findings.numbers: In-sample gross 66 bps/mo; academic (naive) implementation post-publication NET = -3 bps/mo (SE 5). Cost-optimized EW: in-sample net 38, post-pub 13, post-pub & post-2005 = 8 bps/mo (SE 4). Cost-optimized VALUE-WEIGHTED post-pub & post-2005 = 4 bps/mo (SE 3). Strongest anomalies after data-mining adjustment: 10-20 bps/mo. Post-publication decay 50%, rising to 72% excluding pre-2005 data and 93% after trading costs. Cost mechanics: typical anomaly 2-sided monthly turnover 30% (15% each side) x average paid spread 111 bps = 32-33 bps/mo return reduction. Modern spread reality: 2014 mean spread PAID by anomaly strategies 67 bps vs average NYSE spread 16 bps, NYSE modal spread ~5 bps, ~20% of NYSE stocks above 20 bps. Critical methodological correction: Hasbrouck low-frequency spreads (used by Novy-Marx & Velikov) are 'biased upward by 25-50 basis points' post-2003.

key_findings.claim: Best available peer-reviewed MEASUREMENT of the modern US large-cap spread: S&P 500 effective spread averages 3.22 bps (dollar-weighted, 506 stocks, 55.7M trades). Because effective spread is defined as TWICE the trade-to-midpoint distance, the one-way cost of a small liquidity-demanding order in an S&P 500 name is ~1.6 bps. This is the correct anchor for pyfinagent's scale, NOT the 50-111 bps figures in the anomaly literature (which are full-CRSP, microcap-inclusive, low-frequency-estimator numbers).
key_findings.numbers: Dec 7-11 2015, S&P 500: midpoint effective spread mean 3.22 bps (median 3.02; 5th pct 1.64; 95th pct 7.78; SD 2.18). Micro-price ('true') effective spread mean 2.73 bps. Quoted spread mean 3.55 bps (median 3.23). Midpoint measure is biased +18% on average (nominal 0.49 bps, t=9.76), up to 97% for sub-$15 stocks. Stocks above $50 = 74% of S&P 500 dollar volume, effective spreads 'around 2.1 bps'. Mean trade price $119.27; median stock dollar volume $424M/day. => one-way cost = 3.22/2 = 1.61 bps (midpoint) or 2.73/2 = 1.37 bps (micro-price).

key_findings.claim: Live institutional execution data ($1.7trn, 21 markets, 1998-2016) shows real costs are an order of magnitude below TAQ-model estimates, and that market impact is a function of trade size as %DTV — which at pyfinagent's scale rounds to zero. Their model validates against actual index-fund costs almost exactly. Also: LONG-ONLY trading is MORE expensive per trade than long-short because there is no netting — directly relevant since pyfinagent is long-only.
key_findings.numbers: All trades: mean market impact 9.97 bps, mean implementation shortfall 11.02 bps; median MI 6.18 / IS 8.63; dollar-weighted mean MI 15.14 / IS 16.06. Large cap 8.90 bps MI vs small cap 18.95 bps. Long-only 13.7 bps MI vs long-short 8.4 bps. By trade size (their calibrated model vs TAQ models): at 2% of DTV 13.73 bps (TAQ-linear says 44.89, TAQ-sqrt 27.09); at 10% of DTV 32.34 bps (TAQ models 60.23 / 64.21). Validation: actual S&P 500 index-fund annual cost 4.72 bps, their model predicts 4.81 bps; Russell 2000 actual 12.87 bps, model 12.36 bps (linear-TAQ model predicts 29.79 / 155.79 — 6x and 12x too high). Firm cross-section: 10th pct 8.68 bps, median 14.55 bps, 90th pct 38.1 bps. 85% of price impact is permanent (only 1.26 bps of ~9 bps reverses in 24h).

key_findings.claim: The cost law is exactly linear in turnover, verified on live executions: realized annual cost = 12 x monthly two-sided turnover x per-trade market impact. Capacity therefore falls inversely with turnover — the highest-turnover strategy (short-term reversal, the closest analogue to a fast headline signal) has one-tenth the capacity of value/momentum and is only marginally significant net.
key_findings.numbers: US 1998-2011, $699.6bn of $721.4bn traded was LARGE CAP. SMB: TO 50%/mo, cost 1.46%/yr, MI 24.2 bps, net 1.16%/yr (t=5.20), break-even $103bn. HML: TO 68%, cost 1.54%/yr, MI 19 bps, net 2.34%/yr (t=10.20), break-even $83bn. UMD: TO 127%, cost 3.51%/yr, MI 23 bps, net 4.34%/yr (t=8.42), break-even $52bn. STR (short-term reversal): TO 305%/mo, cost 6.75%/yr, MI 18.4 bps, net 1.52%/yr (t=2.14 only), break-even just $9.5bn. ValMom: TO 79% (netting benefit), cost 2.18%/yr, net 4.05%/yr (t=13.11), break-even $98bn. All four combined: TO 102%, cost 2.39%/yr, MI 19.4 bps, net 3.00%/yr (t=11.37). Arithmetic check: 12 x 3.05 x 18.4bp = 673 bps = the reported 6.75%/yr, exact.

key_findings.claim: RECENCY SCAN (2024, 1972-2022 sample): naively-constructed momentum is a coin flip net of costs — 63 bps/month of trading costs against a 0.64%/month gross premium leaves 0.01%/month. Cost-aware construction halves the cost and multiplies net return 22-fold. This independently reproduces Novy-Marx & Velikov's mid-turnover finding on a modern sample and confirms that HOW a signal is traded matters as much as whether it predicts.
key_findings.numbers: Cost-agnostic momentum: gross 0.64%/mo (highest of all factors considered), transaction costs 63 bps/mo, NET 0.01%/mo. TCA momentum: 30 bps/mo cost, net return 22x higher, annualized net Sharpe +0.19, MVE weight rises from marginal to >10%. Model ranking flips: Barillas-Shanken 6-factor has the highest gross Sh2 (2.25, 8.4% ahead of second-best) but this is 'largely illusory' once costs enter. Fama-French factors incur 51-55% of annual turnover in NON-reconstitution months (SMB 51.1%, HML 54.1%, RMW 54.8%, CMA 54.8%), i.e. 0.63-0.69% of annual cost is spent outside the intended annual rebalance.

key_findings.claim: DERIVED TURNOVER/COST TABLE for the candidate thematic designs, using T = 2 x rebalances/yr x fraction-of-book-replaced and annual cost = T x one-way-cost. The model reconciles EXACTLY with pyfinagent's own phase-53.1 replay (133 bps/yr) and with Ke/Kelly/Xiu's own published cost figures (46%/yr), so it is not a free-floating estimate.
key_findings.numbers: Columns = T (x NAV/yr one-way) | cost @1.6bp | @3bp | @10bp(repo default). Continuous rank tilt (incremental, ~8% extra names/mo): T=1.9 | 3 | 6 | 19 bps/yr. Quarterly full thematic basket: T=8.0 | 13 | 24 | 80. MONTHLY top-N, LIVE TODAY (measured 0.555 replaced/mo): T=13.3 | 21 | 40 | 133 bps/yr. Event entry + 8-week time exit: T=13.0 | 21 | 39 | 130. Event entry + 4-week time exit: T=26.0 | 42 | 78 | 260. Weekly rotation: T=104 | 166 | 312 | 1,040. Daily headline (KKX VW 91.4%/day): T=460.7 | 737 | 1,382 | 4,607 bps/yr. Reconciliation 2: KKX daily @10bp = 4,607 bps/yr = 46%/yr, matching 2 x 0.914 x 10 bps/day x 252.

key_findings.claim: THE CROSSOVER, quantified. Max sustainable turnover T = alpha budget / one-way cost. Against Chen-Velikov's measured value-weighted large-cap alpha budget, slow thematic designs clear by 2-10x and daily designs miss by ~20x. Crucially, at the repo's own conservative 10 bps assumption the CURRENTLY-LIVE monthly design already spends 133 bps/yr — nearly 3x the 48 bps/yr central alpha estimate — so a thematic overlay must not be a separate trading sleeve layered on top.
key_findings.numbers: At c=3 bps: alpha 48 bps/yr -> max T=16.0x; alpha 120 -> T=40.0x; alpha 240 -> T=80.0x. At c=1.6 bps: T=30.0 / 75.0 / 150.0x. At c=10 bps (repo): T=4.8 / 12.0 / 24.0x. Live monthly design sits at T=13.3 — inside the budget at c=1.6-3bp on all three alpha assumptions, but at c=10bp it clears ONLY the 'strongest anomaly' (10-20 bps/mo) assumption and fails the average-anomaly one by 2.8x. Daily headline at T=460.7 fails every combination: it needs 1,382 bps/yr of gross alpha at c=3bp, i.e. 5.8x the best-case 240 bps/yr budget and 29x the central 48 bps/yr.

key_findings.claim: Banding / buy-hold spread is the literature's single most effective simple cost-mitigation technique, and pyfinagent already implements it — but at our cost level the prize is only ~8-16 bps/yr, which is why phase-53.1's REJECT is correct even though the phase-53.1 reasoning under-diagnosed it as an effect-size failure rather than a statistical-power failure.
key_findings.numbers: Novy-Marx & Velikov sS 10%/20% rule vs plain decile sort across the 23 anomalies: average turnover reduction 41%, transaction cost reduction 42%. Momentum: TO 34.52 -> 18.82 %/mo, cost 65 -> 35 bps/mo, net return 0.68 -> 0.85 %/mo (t 2.45 -> 3.35). ValMomProf net 0.99 -> 1.02 (t=6.19). Reduced-frequency rebalancing by contrast gives 'roughly only a one-third reduction in turnover and transaction cost'; the FAJ 2019 follow-up finds quarterly rebalancing's gross-performance decline is of similar magnitude to its cost saving, i.e. NO net benefit on average. pyfinagent measured (backend/backtest/rebalance_band.py, 48 monthly S&P 500 rebalances 2022-2025, top_n=10, band 0.2): turnover 0.555 -> 0.489 (12% cut), gross Sharpe 1.388 -> 1.399, net 1.351 -> 1.366, dSharpe +0.015 p=0.376 CI90 [-0.066,+0.092] -> REJECT. Available saving at c=3bp: (13.3-11.7) x 3 = ~5 bps/yr; at c=10bp ~16 bps/yr — far below the detection floor of a 48-month Sharpe-difference test.

negative_or_null_results: KKX NEVER publish a value-weighted net-of-transaction-cost result. Their entire net-of-cost analysis (Table 5) is explicitly equal-weighted. Their VW long-short is 10 bps/day gross at 91.4% daily turnover; applying their OWN 10 bps convention gives -8.28 bps/day (~-21%/yr). The widely-cited 'profitable net of costs' claim does not transfer to a large-cap universe.
KKX VW short leg: gross 1 bp/day, annualized Sharpe 0.04. The value-weighted news strategy is essentially a long-only trade with no short-side contribution.

Chen & Velikov: cost-optimized VALUE-WEIGHTED anomalies, post-publication and post-2005, expect 4 bps/month with SE 3 bps — statistically indistinguishable from zero. Naive academic implementations expect -3 bps/month. Post-publication decay is 50%, 72% excluding pre-2005 data, and 93% after trading costs.

Novy-Marx & Velikov high-turnover panel: 4 of 6 strategies have NEGATIVE net returns (Industry Momentum -0.29 t=-1.20; Industry Relative Reversals -0.80 t=-4.73; Short-run Reversals -1.28 t=-6.02; Seasonality -0.62 t=-3.88). The two survivors (High-frequency Combo +0.16 t=1.11; Low-Vol Industry Relative Reversals +0.19 t=1.41) are NOT statistically significant.

Baldi-Lanfranchi (2024, 1972-2022): cost-agnostic momentum's 0.64%/month gross premium becomes 0.01%/month net after 63 bps/month of trading costs. Momentum, the flagship mid-turnover anomaly, is a coin flip when traded naively.

Reducing rebalance frequency does NOT work as a standalone cost fix. Novy-Marx & Velikov: quarterly rebalancing gives 'roughly only a one-third reduction in turnover and transaction cost, as more of the portfolio turns over at each rebalance point', and the FAJ 2019 follow-up finds the gross-performance decline offsets the saving — no net benefit on average.

Restricting to cheap-to-trade (liquid) stocks is also naive: per Chen & Velikov's summary of Novy-Marx & Velikov (2019), 'the reduction in gross returns is as large or larger than the improvement in trading costs'. Liquidity screening is not free alpha.

Equal-weighting is a cost trap. Novy-Marx & Velikov: EW transaction costs are 'two to three times as high' as VW, and EW results 'are misleading and should be viewed skeptically... equal-weighting often results in a deterioration of net performance'.

pyfinagent's OWN phase-53.1 banding experiment: dSharpe +0.015, p=0.376, CI90 [-0.066,+0.092] -> REJECT. Directionally favourable, statistically null. My reading is that this was a POWER failure (the available saving is ~5-16 bps/yr, undetectable in 48 monthly observations by a Sharpe-difference test), not evidence that banding fails — but the REJECT verdict stands regardless because the prize is too small to matter at our cost level.

Novy-Marx & Velikov's cost figures are systematically too high for a 2026 large-cap application: Chen & Velikov show the Hasbrouck low-frequency spread estimator NM&V rely on is 'biased upward by 25-50 basis points' after 2003. Do not import NM&V's 50%-monthly-turnover threshold as a hard rule without re-deriving it at modern large-cap spreads.

NEGATIVE METHOD RESULT: no free, publicly-fetchable, MEASURED 2025-2026 US large-cap effective spread figure could be obtained. Alpha Vantage's REALTIME_BULK_BID_ASK_PRICES is a premium endpoint and returned data explicitly labelled 'ARTIFICIAL AND FOR ILLUSTRATION PURPOSES ONLY' (I did not use it). NYSE's daily market statistics page publishes consolidated quoted spreads but gave no figures. The SEC MIDAS individual-security metrics (free, ~9,200 securities, includes effective spread, coverage through at least Jan 2025) is the obvious free source and was NOT ingested. The modern anchor therefore remains Hagstromer's Dec-2015 S&P 500 measurement.

Long-only is MORE expensive per trade than long-short: 13.7 bps vs 8.4 bps of market impact in the AQR live-execution data, because long-short books net offsetting trades. pyfinagent is long-only, so it forgoes the ValMom-style netting benefit that took that combination's break-even capacity to $98bn versus $83bn/$52bn standalone.

Molchanov & Stangl (IJFE 2024) 'The myth of business cycle sector rotation' finds sector-rotation outperformance 'quickly diminishes after allowing for transaction costs' and reports limited evidence of systematic industry performance over business cycles. NOT read in full — both the AUT and Wiley hosts returned HTTP 403. Treated as a flagged caution, not as evidence.
recommendation_for_pyfinagent: Build the thematic channel as a SCORE OVERLAY on the existing monthly reconstitution — the exact shape of the 14 existing apply_*_to_score functions routed through overlay_math.py::sign_safe_mult — and NOT as a separate event-triggered trading sleeve. Incremental turnover T is then ~1.9x NAV/yr and incremental cost is 3-19 bps/yr, a rounding error against any plausible alpha. Concretely: (1) Add the theme score as a multiplicative tilt on the existing rank, so it can only reorder names near the top-N boundary; it must never open a position the base score would not have ranked. (2) If an event-triggered sleeve is genuinely wanted instead, hard-bind it to a MINIMUM HOLDING PERIOD of >= 8 weeks with a TIME-BASED exit, never a signal-based exit — a signal-based exit makes turnover a function of signal noise and is the single mechanism that converts a slow thematic design into a fast one. That caps T at ~13x, i.e. 39 bps/yr at c=3bp, and it is also the guardrail FINSABER named and that the repo already recorded in phase-55.3 as the evidence-best LEVER. (3) Fix the cost calibration so the gate is honest: backtest_engine.py:171 and backtest_trader.py:53 both default transaction_cost_pct=0.1 (10 bps one-way, 20 bps round-trip) and scripts/ablation/no_trade_band_replay.py:39 hardcodes ROUND_TRIP_COST=0.002. Against the measured S&P 500 one-way half-spread of ~1.6 bps that is ~6x conservative. Do not silently lower it — instead make it an explicit sweep parameter and report every new design's net result at c in {1.6, 3, 10} bps, because a design that only passes at 1.6 bps is not robust and a design that fails only at 10 bps is being rejected by an assumption rather than by evidence. (4) Ingest SEC MIDAS individual-security metrics (free, ~9,200 securities, monthly effective spread) as a small step so the cost parameter becomes a MEASUREMENT rather than a citation to a Dec-2015 sample — this is the one cheap action that removes the largest remaining uncertainty in this lens. (5) Do NOT reopen the banding/hysteresis question: at c=3bp the entire available saving is ~5 bps/yr, which no Sharpe-difference test on a 48-month sample can detect; the phase-53.1 REJECT and the score-hysteresis ban should stand. (6) Reframe the promotion gate for the thematic work: since cost clears comfortably for any weeks-to-months design, the binding constraint is the DSR>=0.95 / PBO<=0.5 / beat-incumbent-OOS alpha gate, and the next cycle's effort belongs there, not on cost engineering.
rejected_options: REJECTED ON COST — Daily or near-daily headline-drift trading of the universe. T = 460.7x NAV/yr one-way; cost 737 bps/yr at c=1.6bp, 1,382 bps/yr at c=3bp, 4,607 bps/yr (46%/yr) at the repo's c=10bp. It needs 1,382 bps/yr of gross alpha at c=3bp versus an empirically measured value-weighted large-cap alpha budget of 48-240 bps/yr — a miss of 6x against the best case and 29x against the central case. Ke/Kelly/Xiu's own value-weighted numbers go to -8.28 bps/day at their own 10 bps assumption. This confirms the operator's prior decision to scope fast headline drift OUT, with a number attached.

REJECTED ON COST — Weekly rotation of the whole book. T = 104x NAV/yr; cost 166 bps/yr at c=1.6bp, 312 bps/yr at c=3bp, 1,040 bps/yr at c=10bp. At c=3bp it exceeds even the 240 bps/yr best-case alpha budget by 1.3x, and at the repo's own cost assumption it exceeds it by 4.3x. Nothing in the measured large-cap alpha distribution supports a weekly turnover budget.

REJECTED ON MECHANISM — Signal-based exit (exit when the theme score decays) without a minimum holding period. This makes T a function of signal volatility rather than of a chosen holding period, and is precisely how a design whose intent is 8-week holds ends up trading weekly. Novy-Marx & Velikov's short-term-reversal result (TO 305%/mo, cost 6.75%/yr, capacity only $9.5bn) is the empirical shape of this failure.

REJECTED — Equal-weighting the thematic basket across the full 500-1000 name universe. Novy-Marx & Velikov measure EW transaction costs at 'two to three times as high' as value-weighted, because EW pulls the basket into the illiquid tail; they conclude EW results 'often result in a deterioration of net performance'. Cap-weight or liquidity-screen within the basket.

REJECTED — Reducing rebalance frequency (monthly -> quarterly) as a standalone cost-mitigation lever. Novy-Marx & Velikov measure only a one-third turnover reduction, and their FAJ 2019 follow-up finds the resulting gross-performance decline is of similar magnitude to the saving, i.e. no net benefit on average. Quarterly cadence is fine as a DESIGN choice for a slow signal; it is not a fix for a fast one.

REJECTED — Reopening banding / no-trade bands / score-hysteresis as a way to make a higher-turnover thematic design affordable. The literature's 41-42% turnover-and-cost reduction is real, but applied to our cost level it saves ~5 bps/yr at c=3bp and ~16 bps/yr at c=10bp. That is below any detectable effect size on the available sample, and the repo already measured p=0.376 and banned the family.

REJECTED AS A DATA SOURCE — Alpha Vantage REALTIME_BULK_BID_ASK_PRICES for a live spread measurement. It is a premium endpoint; the free response is explicitly labelled 'THE SAMPLE DATA SCHEMA BELOW IS ARTIFICIAL AND FOR ILLUSTRATION PURPOSES ONLY' and returns a fixed 2024-10-18 sample. Using it would violate the $0-metered constraint or produce a fabricated measurement.

CONSIDERED AND NOT ADOPTED — Importing Novy-Marx & Velikov's '50% one-sided monthly turnover' as a hard design rule. It was calibrated on 1963-2012 full-CRSP costs of roughly 68-99 bps round-trip using a low-frequency spread estimator that Chen & Velikov show is biased upward by 25-50 bps post-2003. Our measured large-cap round-trip is ~3.2 bps, roughly 20-30x lower, so the threshold must be re-derived at our cost level rather than transplanted — which is what the T-budget table above does.
open_questions: What is the actual 2025-2026 measured effective spread for our specific universe? The anchor used here (Hagstromer, S&P 500, 3.22 bps) is a Dec-2015 sample. SEC MIDAS publishes free per-security monthly effective spreads for ~9,200 securities with coverage through at least Jan 2025 and was not ingested. Until it is, the cost parameter is a citation, not a measurement — the exact failure mode the memory 'measure, don't assert' names.

Is backtest_engine.py's transaction_cost_pct=0.1 (10 bps one-way) deliberate conservatism or an unexamined default? It is ~6x the measured S&P 500 half-spread and it silently biases every ON/OFF ablation gate against higher-turnover designs by that factor. Nothing found in the code or handoff record documents the derivation.

What is the incremental turnover of a theme overlay in practice? The 8%/month figure used for the continuous-tilt row is an ESTIMATE, not a measurement. It is directly measurable at $0 by replaying the existing monthly reconstitution with and without a candidate overlay and differencing the basket membership — the same harness scripts/ablation/no_trade_band_replay.py already uses.

What is the gross alpha of the slow thematic channel? Every finding here says cost is not the binding constraint for a weeks-to-months design, which means this lens cannot approve or reject the thematic idea — only the alpha gate can. No source read here measures a cross-sector theme-to-beneficiary signal's gross return.

Version reconciliation on Ke/Kelly/Xiu: the NBER w26186 rev1 I read reports EW L-S Sharpe 4.29 and 33 bps/day, while search results for a published version cite an annualized 35.56% return and Sharpe 2.21. Different sample or specification; not reconciled. All figures quoted here are from the NBER revision.

Long-only versus long-short: all the cost-vs-turnover literature is long-short. pyfinagent is long-only, which halves the traded notional for a given signal but forgoes the netting benefit AQR measured (long-only 13.7 bps market impact vs long-short 8.4 bps). Whether the T-budget derived here should be tightened or loosened for a long-only book was not resolved.

Sector-rotation null results could not be read in full — both hosts for Molchanov & Stangl (IJFE 2024) returned HTTP 403, as did the MDPI 2026 TSX-60 rebalancing-frequency study and the 2025 ScienceDirect European news-sentiment paper (which snippets suggest reports that value-weighted sentiment profitability 'declines fast after one month' and that gains for LARGE-CAP long-short sentiment portfolios are 'limited'). That last one is directly on-lens and worth a retry through another host.

lens: LENS 5 — Free-source feasibility under the $0 metered hard constraint. Six-axis assessment (history depth, latency, rate limit, point-in-time integrity, derived-signal licence, single-machine extraction cost) of GDELT, SEC EDGAR, Alpaca news, Alpha Vantage NEWS_SENTIMENT, Caldara-Iacoviello GPR, FRED, and Wikimedia pageviews. Findings are predominantly MEASURED against the live APIs/BigQuery on 2026-08-04, not read from vendor docs.
bottom_line: Free data does NOT cap the row count — GDELT gives 4,169 measured days of theme intensity, GPR 41 years, EDGAR 25 years, all deep enough to clear DSR/PBO arithmetically. What free data caps is the FIRM-LEVEL news layer, and two of the three candidate sources there are disqualified on grounds that have nothing to do with sample size: Alpha Vantage is licence-blocked for exactly our use ("personal, non-commercial use", with "investment analysis, research, testing" named as commercial) and its pre-2026 archive is a thin retroactive backfill (AAPL: 53 articles in Jan-2025 vs >=1000 in Jan-2026, a >=19x density discontinuity that makes it PIT-invalid for backtesting), plus a MEASURED hard limit of "25 requests per day". The honest binding constraint is not bytes but INDEPENDENT THEMATIC EPISODES: ~23-46 in GDELT's 11.46-year window at 2-4 big cross-sector themes/year — and no amount of paid data fixes that, because it is a property of the world. Recommended free stack: GDELT gkg_partitioned for theme intensity (peer-reviewed literature explicitly endorses GDELT for exactly this aggregate use and warns against event-level use), GPR for the geopolitical episodes, and SEC EDGAR full-text search as the theme->beneficiary mapping substrate — EDGAR is the only candidate that is simultaneously deep, PIT-clean, public-domain, firm-level and $0.

key_findings.claim: GDELT's licence is fully permissive for derived commercial signals — no blocker. Verbatim: "all datasets released by the GDELT Project are available for unlimited and unrestricted use for any academic, commercial, or governmental use of any kind without fee." Attribution + link to gdeltproject.org required.
key_findings.numbers: $0 fee; unlimited commercial use; attribution required. Event database coverage from 1979-01-01 per docs; MEASURED min MonthYear=192001, max=202608 in gdelt-bq.gdeltv2.events.

key_findings.claim: THE DECISIVE GDELT ANSWER: the peer-reviewed literature explicitly endorses GDELT for aggregate/macro theme-intensity use and warns against firm/event-level use — exactly the distinction the lens asked about. Verbatim: "GDELT is suitable for macro-level early warning scenarios requiring high recall, while POLECAT is better suited for tasks requiring high signal-to-noise ratio inputs" and "In scenarios prioritizing the capture of macro trends and high recall rates, GDELT should be the preferred choice... However, corresponding deduplication and noise-reduction filtering algorithms must be designed in the model's backend to control the false positive rate."
key_findings.numbers: GDELT positive recall 0.111 at one city node (missing ~89% of actual protest events); precision fell to 0.144 at high-frequency nodes; POLECAT negative recall 0.904 at Manila/Cairo. POLECAT gold standard = 1000 human double/triple-reviewed samples spanning Jan 2001-Dec 2020. Train/val/test split 60:20:20 chronological.

key_findings.claim: GDELT's documented ~55% accuracy is a per-EVENT-RECORD figure that largely averages out in an aggregate theme series, but the ~20% redundancy is a BIAS not noise (duplicate stories scale with virality, which is precisely what a theme-intensity signal keys on) — so deduplication is mandatory, not optional.
key_findings.numbers: Key-field accuracy ~55% overall; English ~56%, non-English ~53%. Methodology: 400 event records, 3 researchers independently reviewing original text. Redundancy measured on US 2021 data, 48 sampled days (1st/7th/14th/21st of each month): 6,640,748 total event records vs 1,367,141 duplicates = ~20.6%. Author-stated limitation verbatim: "The accuracy audit was conducted on a sample from a single year (2021) and may not fully capture temporal variations in GDELT's machine coding performance."

key_findings.claim: MEASURED (bq dry-run, 2026-08-04): the naive GDELT theme query violates the $0 constraint by itself, but the partitioned table rescues it by ~4,957x. A single `SELECT DATE, V2Themes FROM gdelt-bq.gdeltv2.gkg LIMIT 10` scans 1.88 TB — LIMIT does NOT reduce BigQuery cost, and that one query is 1.88x the entire 1 TiB/month free tier.
key_findings.numbers: gdeltv2.gkg V2Themes = 1,880,275,196,389 bytes (1.88 TB). gkg_partitioned + _PARTITIONTIME single day = 379,407,179 bytes (379 MB). One month = 11,523,200,208 bytes (11.5 GB). COUNT(*) on partitioned = 0 bytes (metadata only). Daily incremental 379 MB/day = ~11.4 GB/month, ~90x inside the 1 TiB free tier. Full 11.46y backfill = 4,169 days x 379 MB = ~1.58 TB = ~$3.60 one-time at $6.25/TiB, or two months of free tier.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: GDELT GKG theme history depth is 2015-02-17 to 2026-08-04 with 4,169 distinct daily partitions (~99.6% calendar completeness). This covers all four operator reference cases (COVID 2020, AI/datacenter 2023, Ukraine 2022, Iran/oil 2024-25).
key_findings.numbers: min _PARTITIONTIME = 2015-02-17, max = 2026-08-04, COUNT(DISTINCT DATE(_PARTITIONTIME)) = 4169. Span 11.46 years. Update cadence 15 minutes (masterfilelist confirms 20260804090000.gkg.csv.zip); masterfilelist has 1,183,308 lines with per-file MD5.

key_findings.claim: BLOCKER — Alpha Vantage's licence forbids our exact use case. Verbatim: "Alpha Vantage grants the right to install, use, access, display and run the software... for personal, non-commercial use, unless you and Alpha Vantage have agreed otherwise in writing." Commercial use is triggered by criterion (i): "You intend to use the Alpha Vantage Platform for any purpose that goes beyond personal usage including investment analysis, research, testing, monitoring." Investment analysis, research and testing are NAMED as commercial.
key_findings.numbers: 4-page Terms of Service PDF read in full. Governed by Massachusetts law. Commercial licensing via premium@alphavantage.co. Clause 20 notes the Economic Indicators/Commodities APIs are themselves FRED-derived and bind the user to FRED's terms.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED CORRECTION to the brief: Alpha Vantage NEWS_SENTIMENT actually reaches back to 2010-01-05, not 2022-02-24. But this is a trap, not a win — the pre-2026 archive is a thin retroactive backfill with a >=19x density discontinuity vs the live feed, making it point-in-time INVALID for backtesting.
key_findings.numbers: AAPL articles returned per January (limit=1000, so items = true population): 2010=18, 2013=5, 2016=23, 2019=26, 2020=27, 2021=84, 2022=65, 2023=66, 2024=49, 2025=53, 2026>=1000 (capped). Earliest record returned with sort=EARLIEST from 2005: 2010-01-05T11:50:00, source CBC, relevance 0.729231, sentiment -0.219448. key_findings.claim: MEASURED, verbatim from the live API: Alpha Vantage free-tier limit is "our standard API rate limit is 25 requests per day" — not the 5/min-500/day figure still repeated in many secondary sources. This makes universe-scale backfill arithmetically impossible.
key_findings.numbers: Hit after ~16 calls in one session. At 25 req/day, a 500-ticker universe needs >=20 days at a physically impossible 1 call/ticker; realistically many calls/ticker (limit caps at 1000 items) implies 400+ days for a single backfill. Infeasible.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: Alpaca news archive floor is 2015-01-05 (2014 returns 0 rows, 2015 returns data), confirming the documented "back to 2015". Source is Benzinga verbatim: "All news data is currently provided directly by Benzinga." But article BODY text is unavailable for the archive on our access, and the licence for derived signals is unresolved.
key_findings.numbers: LMT probe: 2010=0, 2014=0, 2015 earliest=2015-01-05T12:11:20Z, 2016=2016-01-04T12:46:35Z, 2020=2020-01-06T12:32:33Z. include_content=true on 2016 rows returned hasContent=False (headlines only). `source` field returns empty string, not "Benzinga". LMT 2023 >= 300 articles over 6 pages (probe capped). Rate limit 200 calls/min free plan, limit max 50/page. ~130+ articles/day across the whole universe.

key_findings.claim: GPR is the cleanest news-derived source available: CC-BY licensed (derived commercial signals explicitly permitted) AND it publishes dated VINTAGES, which is best-in-class point-in-time hygiene for a news index. Licence verbatim: "completely open access under the Creative Commons BY license. You have the permission to use, distribute, and reproduce these in any medium, provided the source and authors are credited."
key_findings.numbers: Recent GPR: 10 newspapers, starts 1985. Historical GPR: 3 newspapers, starts 1900. 44 country-specific indexes. 8 categories; GPRT = categories 1-5 (threats), GPRA = categories 6-8 (acts). Monthly updated at start of month; daily updated every Monday (both last updated 2026-08-03). Vintage files: data_gpr_export_YYYYMM.xls, data_gpr_daily_recent_YYYYMMDD.xls. Canonical paper: Caldara & Iacoviello (2022), "Measuring Geopolitical Risk", American Economic Review, April, 112(4), pp.1194-1225.

key_findings.claim: GPR DOES silently revise published history — using the live file instead of the dated vintage introduces lookahead. Verbatim: "The latest data are preliminary and subject to revisions since some newspapers are added to the search database with delay. Additionally, in some cases there could be minor revisions of the data extending further back when duplicate or missing articles or newspaper editions are removed from or added to the database." There is ALSO a methodology break: "The search terms of the index were last changed in 2021 and incorporate a slightly different methodology relative to the old (2018) index (GPR_OLD)."
key_findings.numbers: Two distinct PIT hazards: (1) rolling back-revision of published values, (2) a 2021 search-term/methodology break splitting the series. Daily series updates only WEEKLY (every Monday), so a daily decision cycle faces up to 7 days of staleness on the daily GPR.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: SEC EDGAR full-text search is live, free, unauthenticated, and its coverage floor is 2001 — and it is the ONLY candidate that is simultaneously deep, PIT-clean, public-domain, firm-level and $0. Filings are immutable once accessioned, giving the best point-in-time integrity of any source assessed.
key_findings.numbers: efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index hits by year for "competition": 1999=6, 2000=12, 2001=10000 (capped), 2002=10000, 2004=10000 -> floor is 2001. "geopolitical risk" in 10-Ks: 2015=19, 2021=25; all forms=729. 12 rapid sequential requests all returned HTTP 200 (no throttling observed). Documented fair-access limit 10 req/s = 864,000 req/day, ~1000x more than a 500-1000 ticker daily cycle needs.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: SEC enforces its User-Agent fair-access rule — a request with an empty User-Agent returns HTTP 403 while the identical request with a declared UA returns 200. Any ingestion code must set a declaring User-Agent or it will silently fail.
key_findings.numbers: no-UA request -> HTTP 403. Declared UA ('name email') -> HTTP 200 on all 12 test requests. This matches the existing note in AGENTS.md:147.

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: FRED offers TRUE point-in-time via ALFRED vintages — 1,221 distinct vintage dates for INDPRO reaching back to 1927-01-26. This is the correct way to avoid macro-revision lookahead, and materially better than the vacuous-guard pattern already burned into this codebase's memory.
key_findings.numbers: INDPRO vintage_dates count=1221; first five 1927-01-26, 1927-02-28, 1927-03-28, 1927-04-28, 1927-05-27; latest three 2026-07-17, 2026-06-15, 2026-05-15. Rate test: 30 sequential calls in 10.1s (~3/s) -> 30 OK, 0 errors, no 429. Documented ~120 req/min with an API key (30 without).

key_findings.claim: MEASURED: Wikimedia pageviews per-article data starts 2015-07-01 — NOT 2015-05 and not the 2007 window the founding finance paper used. No API key required and no throttling observed. This means the canonical Moat et al. result CANNOT be replicated on the modern API.
